tips.title: Tourist tips
tips.tagline: Getting around, paying, tipping and staying comfortable in New York.

subway.title: Subway and OMNY
items: Tap a contactless card, phone or watch on the OMNY reader at the turnstile or on the bus. No MetroCard needed.
Use the same card or device every time: after 12 paid rides in a 7-day window, the rest of that week's rides are free.
Transfers between subway and bus within two hours are free when you tap the same card.
Uptown means north, downtown means south. Check the sign on the platform or entrance before you swipe in.
Local trains stop at every station; express trains skip some. The sign on the front and side of the train says which it is.
The subway runs 24/7, but nights and weekends often have service changes. Check before you go.

tipping.title: Tipping and tax
items: Sit-down restaurants: 18 to 22 percent of the pre-tax bill is standard.
Bars: about $1 to $2 per drink, or about 20 percent on a tab.
Counter service and coffee: tipping is optional; a dollar or two is appreciated.
Taxis and rideshares: 15 to 20 percent.
Listed prices usually exclude sales tax, which is added at the register (8.875 percent in New York City).

safety.title: Safety and etiquette
items: Let riders off the train before you board, and do not lean on the doors.
On escalators, stand on the right and walk on the left.
Keep bags zipped and phones in hand, not in back pockets, in crowds.
An empty car on a busy train usually has a reason. Pick another car.
Emergencies: call 911. City services and non-emergency questions: call 311.

summer.body: Free outdoor concerts and movies in parks, and public beaches open from Memorial Day weekend to Labor Day.

fall.title: Fall
fall.body: Foliage in the parks, the Village Halloween Parade on October 31, and the New York City Marathon in early November.

winter.title: Winter
winter.body: Holiday windows and lights, outdoor ice rinks, and the New Year's Eve ball drop in Times Square.

airports.title: Getting here from the airports
items: From JFK: ride the AirTrain to Jamaica (E, J and Z trains, or the LIRR) or to Howard Beach (A train). The AirTrain fare is paid when you exit.
From LaGuardia: the Q70 LaGuardia Link bus runs to the subway at Jackson Heights–Roosevelt Avenue and to the LIRR at Woodside.
From Newark: AirTrain Newark connects to Newark Liberty International Airport Station, with NJ Transit and Amtrak trains to New York Penn Station.
Yellow taxis charge a flat fare between JFK and Manhattan, plus tolls and tip. Check the current amount before you ride.
Take taxis only from the official lines outside arrivals, and ignore anyone inside the terminal offering a ride.

blurbs.soho: Cast-iron buildings, cobblestones and flagship shopping.

blurbs.west-village: Crooked tree-lined streets, jazz clubs and a slice on every corner.
blurbs.union-square: A busy crossroads with a greenmarket, bookstores and subway lines in every direction.
blurbs.meatpacking-district: Old warehouses turned boutiques, the south end of the High Line and the Hudson waterfront.
blurbs.chelsea: Galleries, Chelsea Market and the High Line overhead.
blurbs.nomad: Grand old hotels, rooftop bars and Madison Square Park next door.
blurbs.koreatown: A block of 32nd Street packed with barbecue, karaoke and late-night soup.
blurbs.midtown: Times Square, Broadway theaters and the skyscrapers you have seen in movies.

blurbs.upper-west-side: Museums, brownstones and two parks: Central on one side, Riverside on the other.
blurbs.upper-east-side: Museum Mile along Fifth Avenue and quiet townhouse blocks.
blurbs.harlem: Soul food, jazz history and the Apollo on 125th Street.
blurbs.williamsburg: Waterfront parks, rooftop bars, coffee roasters and weekend food markets.
blurbs.greenpoint: Polish bakeries, vintage shops and quiet streets along the East River.
blurbs.dumbo: Cobblestones between two bridges, and the most photographed view in Brooklyn.
blurbs.brooklyn-heights: Brownstone streets above the harbor and a promenade facing Lower Manhattan.
blurbs.park-slope: Brownstones, family cafés and the edge of Prospect Park.
blurbs.bushwick: Warehouse murals, galleries and late-night bars.
blurbs.sunset-park: Brooklyn's Chinatown, taquerias, and a hilltop park looking out over the harbor.
blurbs.flushing: One of the city's biggest Chinatowns: dumplings, food courts and bubble tea.
blurbs.astoria: Greek tavernas, beer gardens and the Museum of the Moving Image.
blurbs.jackson-heights: South Asian and Latin American food along Roosevelt Avenue and 74th Street.
blurbs.long-island-city: Riverfront parks with the best Midtown skyline views, plus MoMA PS1.
blurbs.belmont: The Bronx's Little Italy, centered on Arthur Avenue.
blurbs.mott-haven: Historic rowhouses and a growing arts scene in the South Bronx.
blurbs.st-george: The Staten Island Ferry terminal, with harbor views back to Manhattan.
blurbs.greenwich-village: Washington Square, jazz clubs, old coffeehouses and the streets where the folk revival began.
blurbs.prospect-heights: Brownstone blocks between Prospect Park, the Brooklyn Museum and the Botanic Garden.
blurbs.flushing-meadows: The 1964 World's Fair grounds: the Unisphere, museums and wide lawns next to Citi Field.
blurbs.bronx-park: The Bronx Zoo and the New York Botanical Garden, side by side in the woods along the Bronx River.
blurbs.nolita: Small boutiques, cafés and old Italian bakeries on the tree-lined streets north of Little Italy.
blurbs.hells-kitchen: Theater-district restaurants along Ninth Avenue and the Intrepid on the Hudson.
blurbs.washington-heights: Dominican food and music, The Met Cloisters and cliff-top parks above the Hudson.
blurbs.flatbush: Caribbean bakeries, jerk chicken and roti along Flatbush and Church Avenues.
blurbs.woodside: Little Manila's Filipino restaurants and Irish pubs under the 7 train.
blurbs.tribeca: Wide cobbled streets, converted warehouses and some of the city's most celebrated restaurants.
blurbs.noho: Cast-iron lofts, Bond Street's restaurants and a short walk to both Villages.
blurbs.flatiron: The Flatiron Building, Madison Square Park and a dense run of top restaurants.
blurbs.murray-hill: Quiet townhouse blocks near Grand Central, with classic delis and neighborhood bars.
blurbs.fort-greene: Brownstones around Fort Greene Park, Sunday markets and neighborhood bistros.
blurbs.cobble-hill: Leafy brownstone blocks and Atlantic Avenue's Middle Eastern shops and restaurants.
blurbs.carroll-gardens: Old Italian bakeries, front gardens and a busy restaurant strip along Smith Street.
blurbs.gowanus: Old canal-side warehouses turned into bars, music venues and restaurants.
blurbs.bay-ridge: Middle Eastern and Scandinavian food along Third Avenue, with views of the Verrazzano Bridge.

privacy.title: Privacy
privacy.tagline: What NYCrave keeps, what it sends, and what it never collects.

device.title: Kept on your device
items: Saved places and saved days are stored in your browser's local storage. They never leave your device, and clearing your browser data removes them.
Your light or dark mode choice is stored the same way.
If you install NYCrave, the app keeps a copy of your saved places so they open offline.

location.title: Your location
items: Near me asks your browser for your location only when you tap it.
Distances and walking times are worked out on your device. Your location is never sent to NYCrave or stored.

reports.title: Problem reports
items: When you report a problem with a place, we store the place, the kind of problem and any note you write. There is no name or email field.
To stop floods of reports, the server briefly counts reports per network address in memory. It is not saved.

feedback.title: Feedback
items: When you send feedback, we store your rating, the features you picked, anything you write and the site language. There is no name or email field.
To decide when to ask, your browser counts the pages you have seen and remembers when it last asked. That count stays on your device.

services.title: Services the site uses
items: Map tiles come from OpenFreeMap, so your browser requests them from its servers, as with any online map.
Weather forecasts come from Open-Meteo. NYCrave's server asks for the New York forecast; nothing about you is sent.
When Google Places is switched on, place photos and reviews are fetched by NYCrave's server and shown with Google's attribution.

assistant.title: The assistant
items: Ask NYCrave answers from NYCrave's own data on its server. Questions are not stored.
If AI answers are switched on for the site, questions and the conversation so far are sent to Anthropic, which runs the Claude model, to write the answer. Do not share personal details in the chat.

none.title: What NYCrave never does
items: No accounts, no advertising, no analytics and no tracking cookies.
The only cookie is the sign-in cookie for the editors' admin page.
